newsitem.title: USA: Lilco debentures extend gains on pact news.
newsitem.headline: Lilco debentures extend gains on pact news.

text.p: Long Island Lighting Co debenture spreads tightened more than 15 basis points by midday after news the Long Island Power Authority (LIPA) would acquire "spongy" company assets and assume or refinance $3.6 billion in stranded costs, traders said.
The debt is now a full 100 basis points tighter than quotes prior to December's announcement of the planned merger between Long Island Lighting Co and Brooklyn Union Gas Co, traders added.
In recent trade, Lilco's nine-percent debentures were quoted 117 bid, 110 offered, 15 to 20 basis points tighter on the day.

There remains a question on the ultimate ownership of the debentures, however, since some will go to LIPA and others will stay with the Lilco/Brooklyn Union entity, said Tom Mockler, a utilities analyst at Dillon Read & Co Inc.

"That will be significant," Mockler said. "I would think Lilco would be higher quality, since they will merge with Brooklyn Union, and LIPA will have a ton of debt, the nuclear and spongy regulatory assets."

Separately, Mockler said there was some uncertainty surrounding Lilco mortgage bonds that will all go to LIPA. The bonds have a call price of more than 106, he said, but LIPA appears to have the option to call them at par.
It may be still be advantageous to hold those bonds to capitalize on the high coupons during the 12- to 18-month time period before the deal is finalized, he said.
Lilco and Brooklyn Union said they aimed to complete the deal by the end of the calendar year, he noted.

Under terms of the tentative plan, LIPA would acquire all Lilco transmission, distribution and regulatory assets, and Lilco's share of Nine Mile Point 2 nuclear plant. A Lilco/Brooklyn Union holding company still in the planning stages would include Brooklyn Union operations, Lilco's natural gas distribution system and Lilco's non-nuclear generating assets.

The acquisition would be made through a stock purchase from the new holding company, valued at $2.5 billion, Lilco said. Cash for the acquisition is expected to be raised through the issuance of less-costly tax-exempt debt.
Tax-exempt bonds would also be used to refinance the assumed $3.6 billion in debt, which is related to the never-opened Shoreham nuclear power plant.

While the Brooklyn Union/Lilco merger and the LIPA plan each requires approval of various regulatory agencies, Mockler said he sees few hurdles -- with the exception of the Democratic-influenced Public Authorities Control Board.
That entity essentially has a veto on the plan, Mockler said.

"Democrats aren't looking to allow (Republican New York Governor George Pataki) to take credit for anything they can avoid; but on the other hand they probably don't want fingers pointed at them saying they single-handedly obstructed rate decreases," Mockler added.
